One set of sources cites archaeological and textual indications—such as a 3,000-year-old skeleton at Mount Lykaion and ancient texts mentioning child sacrifices on the mountain—that some interpret as evidence of human sacrifice by ancient Greeks [d2]. Another set frames the practice as largely abandoned or confined to myth and ritual substitution, noting vestigial memories of its discrediting and its appearance in tragedy rather than historical practice [d1][d6]. Additional sources describe ritualized expulsion of individuals as a form of “pharmakos,” which some scholars interpret as a human sacrifice proxy [d3], while other accounts explicitly deny widespread practice [d6].

Given the conflicting opinions and research outcomes in the retrieved evidence, the exact status of human sacrifice among the Ancient Greeks remains contested and cannot be conclusively determined from these sources alone.
